90 participants have gaze data. Two are not analysed: 15265 (excluded participant) and 5272 (13 trials recorded). The sample is 88 participants (None 33, Partial 35, Full 20), 87 of them with questionnaire scores.
The median blink duration is 111 ms.
The median observed share of the trial time is .99 (minimum .74).
The median blink rate over the whole trial is 18.5 per minute (IQR 12.4–29.9).

The blink rate goes with pupil data loss: Spearman ρ = .76 with the share of missing pupil samples, and ρ = −.73 with the share of usable pupil trials (
The pupil exclusion criterion (fewer than 50 % usable pupil trials) applies to three of the 88 participants.
These three blink 34, 44 and 50 times per minute. The median of the others is 18 per minute (Mann-Whitney p = .013).
The pupil sample therefore leaves out participants who blink often.

The feedback pupil couples more strongly with Nexus surprise at higher general-factor scores (

). A blink in a pupil window could bias the window value through the interpolated stretch and the pupil change around the lid closure. The check asks two things:
whether blinks in the pupil windows differ by score, outcome or surprise;
whether the score result changes when blinks are controlled.

Blinks in the pupil windows do not differ with the scores or with Nexus surprise, and blink control leaves the score effect on the feedback-pupil surprise slope at the same size. Blinks do not account for this result. In the attack window, blinks are less frequent on bite trials and more frequent on oddball and transition trials. These event differences enter any attack-window contrast of the outcome types.

Blinks are suppressed while the mosquito approaches and occur in a burst 350–500 ms after the feedback. A bite raises the probability of a blink 250–750 ms after the feedback from .21 to .37 and brings the first blink 86 ms earlier. Oddballs and transitions do not change the post-feedback blink. This bite effect is the candidate defensive blink reflex.

The blink rate is lowest during the net placement and highest in the ISI, and rises over the session. It does not follow the Nexus uncertainty before the attack or the surprise of the outcome after correction.
The general factor and the instruction condition are not associated with any blink measure. Higher STICSA trait scores go with fewer post-feedback blinks after blocked attacks.
Blinks do not account for the stronger coupling of the feedback pupil with surprise at higher general-factor scores. The pupil exclusion criterion removes participants who blink often.
